Again, I would say that this entire strategy issue comes from playing with card
limits. With card limits, barring a few obvious deck designs, you cannot build
decks that are successful enough at one thing to win doing it, so they need to
diversify. With no limits, as you can make literally any deck you want, you
can build decks that are perfectly capable of winning and being completely
single minded. If you want to make a diverse deck, you are perfectly able to,
but if you want to make a very focused deck that wins solely on the virtue of
its one angle, you can do that as well.

Using the pure Rush combat deck as an example (again, because the concept of
Rush decks under NL and under 4CL are so vastly different), you can make a
perfectly effective pure, unadulterated rush deck under NL that is completely
free of Wakes/Untaps of any kind, completely free of intercept of any type,
completely free of bleed bonuses of any kind, and complely free of vote defense
of any kind. Such a deck has one purpose--to directly attack and destroy the
vampires of its predator and prey, in doing so controlling the table enough to
oust its prey while keeping down its predator. In such a deck, Wakes are
generally useless, as they clog up the hand, and without intercept you can't
block stuff anyway, so what it the point in trying? In such a deck votes are
useless, as they tend to clog up the hand, and without titled vampires (or lots
and lots of other votes), you can't pass them anyway, so what is the point in
trying? In such a deck, bleed bonuses do not help you kill your opponent's
vampires, consequently making it harder to kill them, so what is the point?
When your prey has no more vampires, you can bleed with impunity...

Under no limits, you do not have to make completely single minded decks.
Versitile decks are completley viable and competetive as well. I have plenty
of successful decks that are very robust and flexible--a Nosferatu
Intercept/Stealth Bleed/Long Range Combat deck; a Brujah tap/bleed/thrown
objects/blood gain deck; a Protean S:CE/Bleed/Untap/Intercept/Garou deck.
These are all very flexible and have the ability to deal with many things. I
also, however, like to build pure focused Rush decks that do not untap,
intercept, vote, or bleed to any extent. Because of no limits on the cards in
my decks, I can build decks to be both successful as flexible, diverse decks as
well as decks that will be sucessful by virtue of their sheer single mindedness
and focus.

Under Card Limits, you do not have this option (as you have discussed at length
in the above post). Your decks _must_ be diverse (you said so yourself).
Thus, every CL deck will end up looking pretty much the same: It'll have
Wakes, Bleed Bonuses, Weapons, some Intercept, and then some other cards. You
specifically pointed this out--that decks under CL generally need to all be the
same. You find this less boring than the literally infinite deck possibilites
of no limits?

This is an interesting perspective. My thoughts on the matter are
(naturally ;-) a little different. I've played a lot of 'all combat'
decks in my time, and in my experience they can certainly win games,
and even sweep tables.

Since it sounds like you haven't seen combat decks be very effective
in winning games, I'll describe how it works for me. My example deck
(probably my favorite one, and probably the most effective all-combat deck
I've played in terms of VPs) is a NL Brujah Bum's Rush cel/pot combat deck;
generally 90 cards since in my playgroup we use 40 min/90 max deck size
regardless of actual number of players, to keep things simple. (Usually
we have 5 players so it's legit, but we like not having to take cards
out if we accidentally have 4, so we let everyone use 90.)

Anyway, the deck uses something like 15 rush cards, typically 9
Immortal Grapple, around 9 Torn Signposts, 9 Undead Strength, 7 Taste
of Vitae, 3 Blur, a bunch of Flash, some Sideslip, Side Strike, Pursuit;
some Blood Dolls, some Pot and Cel skill cards, and a crypt of average
cap no more than 4 (aided by 2 Jimmy Dunn, the most broken vampire I
know of).

In play, a deck like this survives and wins by essentially controlling
the entire table. That means it's a fairly delicate balancing act to
win games playing something like this. What you usually have to do
is torporize or burn some of your predator's vampires early on as well
as your prey's, in order to make sure you don't lose too much pool to
a bleed deck or offensive vote deck. Doing that makes it your
responsibility to keep your predator weak enough that they won't oust
you, but hopefully not so weak that they'll be easily ousted by your
grandpredator. At the same time, you need to beat up some of your
prey's vampires to keep your prey less than fully effective; ideally
you don't want your prey to ever oust your grandprey, but you do
want them to weaken your grandprey enough that when you oust your
initial prey, your grandprey will be relatively easy pickings.

The pool loss you cause your prey with a deck like this will be largely
based on torporizing his vampires so that he has to keep spending more
pool on bringing out more vampires in order to get anything done. You
can also bleed him for 1 with each of your vampires, of course, but this
is a relatively slow method, and it's usually not a good idea unless
your predator has been almost completely neutralized. It may be
worthwhile when your prey is down to his last few pool, and you can
oust him this turn, but otherwise it's often better to use your vampires
for combat rather than bleeding.

If you can pull off the strategy required, it's not at all out of
reach to get three VPs in a five player game (ousting two people and
being the last player), and I have swept tables from time to time.
It's not as easy to do as it can be playing big-bleed or offensive
vote decks, which remove pool much more directly. But it can certainly
be done. It is also more card-intensive, for sure. There have been
some games where I've run out of cards. But even if it takes 35 cards
to oust each player (I think this is on the high side in my games),
that allows two ousts in 70 cards, and if you're the last player you
have 20 cards left at the end. It's probably more difficult to get
3 VPs without being the last player if you're playing a combat deck,
but certainly not impossible. Keep in mind that you can cause very
large effective pool losses in some circumstances - for example, if
your prey brings out an Inner Circle member, and on your next turn
you Bum's Rush her, Torn Signpost, Immortal Grapple, Undead Strength,
Blur or Flash (for another press), Pulled Fangs, you can neutralize
her before she takes a single action. (This is a 6-card combo, yes,
but it's not at all unlikely in playing a well-designed combat deck -
leave off the final Pulled Fangs and it happens all the time.)

Combat can be a difficult strategy to get VPs out of because it
doesn't directly reduce anyone's pool total. But the challenge
of trying to manage the action of an entire game in order to win
can make it worthwhile. Plus, it's fun to mangle vampires horribly.
;-)

The notion of a "wasted card" is vastly different in NL and CL
environments. If a Rush deck is correctly designed, you don't waste
your cards going to combat - that's all you can do to use them. If
they rescue the vampire, then hunt, they've used 2 minion actions and
1 blood, and that leaves a very weak (1 blood) vampire that you'll
easily send to torpor again.

If I use one action to send your big vamp to torpor with no blood
left, and next turn you rescue him and have him hunt, then I've
effectively tied up two of your vampires with one of mine, plus
they're significantly weaker. Not taking our respective prey/predator
into account, you're not exactly on the winning slope.

Things may be different with a deck that's just supposed to deal one
or two points of aggravated damage, because the blood cost of doing
this usually means it won't be an effective way of doing things.

On the "wasting stealth" issue you've mentioned earlier... you're
either trying to intercept all annoying things, or don't bother trying
at all. If you have a dedicated S&B predator, don't try to intercept
them, take a few big bleeds (it hurts a lot), and rush them. If they
can't unload their Stealth cards because you're not trying to block,
they won't be able to do _anything_. Trying to block will more than
likely fail, and you'll allow them to cycle ther cards.

If you're a "pure rush" deck, your best possible bleed defense is to
rush - and it has the advantage that it's effective against almost any
kind of threat.

That's actually a lot different from my archetype Brujah rush deck. In
a 90-card version it'll probably have 60 combat cards. In a NL rush
deck, your goal is to have good combos go off every combat; in an
effective rush deck, you'll have very substantial cardflow every combat,
and to keep the combat cards coming they have to be a large part of
the deck. Hand-jamming on masters or random support cards is a very
bad thing.

(This is much less the case in more permanents-based decks, eg those
that use lots of weapons, intercept-producing equipment, etc. In
a deck like that, you don't necessarily need to play many combat
cards to be as effective as you'll ever be in combat, so you can
have a lower combat-card percentage and still get acceptable cardflow.
But decks like that seem to be more easily destroyed by their particular
anti-deck, for example something that consistently has +1 intercept to
block equip actions, or something with lots of Immortal Grapples and
maneuvers to make your guns useless. At least, those are the problems
I've had.)

Messages.Author: John Whelan
Messages.Body:
My thoughts on Card Limits are as follows:

I think much of the fun in Jyhad comes from the exploration of the
possibilities involved. I would not wish to play any sort of card limits
consistently, because of all the possibilities that would be left
permanently unexplored.

However, I think that occasional play with card-limits can be interesting,
exciting, and refreshing. If you are going to do this, though, why not go
all the way? 4CL does not go nearly far enough. 2CL seems more like it,
but why not 1CL? I once designed a deck with only one each of any given
card and still occasionally play with it in a NL environment. It rarely
wins, but it always has the advantage of surprise and is never boring to
play. People don't look at the first few cards I play and say "Oh, it's
that deck again!"

So I like the idea the occasional playing of 1CL games for the
unpredictable atmosphere of fun that results.

As a final thought, I would say that a rule that states "no more than x
cards in a deck" is essentially unenforcable. The rule should be "no more
than x cards may be played", with discards counting as plays.

Fortitude is tricky, but thankfully very suceptible to the local meta game. In
enviornments where Rush decks are not in vogue, Fortitude tends to be either
completely absent or fairly low intensity. With not much combat, decks with a
lot of Fortitude will end up getting hand jammed, so they will tend to not have
much. However, if you are playing a good Rush deck and traumatizing your local
play group, pretty soon plenty of Fortitude will show up and shut you down.

Against a deck with tons of Skin of Steel, and you are a Rush deck, there is
not much you can do (but be persistent and hopeful), but this is similar to a
S+B deck trying to bleed an untap/bounce deck, or a Ventrue vote deck sitting
next to an Intercept deck. Sometimes there just isn't much you can do.
However, in most competetive situations where I have used Rush decks, Fortitude
really tended to be pretty low key. People who aren't used to Rush combat will
tend to use S:CE rather than Fortitude to protect the Ventrue, and the Gangrel
will generally use Skin of Rock in preference to Skin of Steel, and Skin of
Rock just isn't enough prevention to stop large or multiple Pot hits (these are
generalizations, but pretty accurate from what I have seen...)

If you have alot of Fortitude around your parts, I gotta wonder why? If people
aren't playing heavy Rush combat, I would think that it would cause hand jam a
lot. The trick is to wait until the Fortitude cycles out of the Environment,
and then bring a Rush deck in.

I bring Rush decks to tournaments relying on the fact that most people don't
fear or understand them, and consequently play decks without heavy Fortitude.
At the Origins game a couple of years ago when my combat deck did pretty well,

A Card-play-limit cannot count discards as plays, for logistical reasons.

That is: due to the few random discards (Dr. Jest, e.g.) and the
corner cases of having to discard (by reduction in hand size, e.g.)
when you have a hand full of cards that you've played at their limit
already this leads to illegal situations which cannot be resolved.
